facts: After fatally shooting a guest in her home following an altercation, respondent Kristina Grier was charged with second degree murder and convicted after a trial in the Superior Court for Pierce County in which her attorney did not request jury instructions on a lesser charge of manslaughter. Grier subsequently appealed her conviction, asserting that her attorney’s failure to request manslaughter instructions constituted ineffective assistance of counsel. The Washington Court of Appeals vacated Grier’s conviction, ruling that Grier had been denied effective assistance of counsel in violation of the 6th Amendment to the United States Constitution and Article I §22 of the Washington State Constitution. The state of Washington appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does the fact that Greer agreed to her attorney’s decision to forgo jury instructions on the lesser offense of manslaughter preclude her from raising an ineffective assistance of counsel claim? If not, did Grier’s attorney’s failure to request manslaughter instructions constitute ineffective assistance of counsel?
conclusions: Chief Justice Madsen’s opinion for a unanimous Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that although the decision to exclude or include lesser offense instructions is ultimately a decision that rests with defense counsel and that Grier’s agreement to forgo manslaughter instructions therefore does not preclude her from raising an ineffective assistance of counsel claim, the decision to forgo manslaughter instructions did not constitute ineffective assistance of counsel as it represented a reasonable tactical decision.

title: Qualcomm, Inc. v. Department of Revenue
facts: Seeking a refund of business and occupation taxes that it had paid under protest, petitioner Qualcomm, Inc. filed suit against the respondent Department of Revenue in the Superior Court for Thurston County, asserting that the satellite tracking service it provides to trucking companies, which allows trucking companies to monitor the location and operation of their vehicles and allows drivers to send and receive messages, constitutes an information service rather than a network telephone service and is therefore subject to a lower business and occupation tax rate. The trial court granted summary judgment for the Department of Revenue, ruling that the service is analogous to a network telephone service. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals affirmed the trial court’s decision. Qualcomm appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Is Qualcomm’s tracking service, which provides both information and the transmission of information, subject to the information service or the network telephone service business and occupation tax rate under Washington Revised Code §82.04.065?
conclusions: Justice Chambers’ opinion for the Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that although Qualcomm’s tracking service provides both information and the transmission of information, the primary purpose of purchasers of the system is to obtain useful information regarding the performance of drivers and equipment and the information transmission aspect of the system cannot function as a useful substitute for drivers’ cellular phones, as reflected in the fact that the system is overwhelmingly utilized for triangulating locations. Thus, the Court held that the system is subject to the information service business and occupation tax rate and that Qualcomm is entitled to a refund of business and occupation taxes paid in excess of this rate.

title: Washington v. Marohl
facts: After forcing Joseph Peterson to the floor during an altercation, causing Peterson to suffer minor injuries, petitioner James Marohl was convicted of second degree assault in the Superior Court for Mason County. Marohl subsequently appealed his conviction, asserting that the floor of the casino in which the altercation occurred was not an instrument or thing likely to produce bodily harm for purposes of establishing second degree assault under Washington Revised Code §9A.36.031(1)(d). The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Marohl's conviction. Marohl appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did Marohl commit second degree assault by using the floor as an instrument or thing likely to produce bodily harm?
conclusions: Justice Sanders opinion for a unanimous Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals and held that insufficient evidence existed to convict Marohl of second degree assault insofar as the floor could not be an instrument or thing likely to produce bodily harm given that under the circumstances of the case it was not likely to produce harm and was not used as a weapon.

title: Washington v. Barber
facts: Pursuant to a plea agreement, petitioner Danny Barber pled guilty to felony driving under the influence in the Superior Court for Kitsap County and was sentenced to a previously agreed upon term of incarceration. After it was subsequently revealed that the sentence imposed was unlawful insofar as it failed to include a term of community custody as required by the felony driving under the influence statute, the respondent state of Washington moved to amend Barber’s sentence and the trial court imposed the mandated term of community custody. Barber appealed the trial court’s amendment of his sentence, asserting that he was entitled to specific performance of the terms of the plea agreement. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed the trial court’s decision. Barber appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Is a defendant entitled to specific performance of a plea agreement that is contrary to law?
conclusions: Justice Stephens’ opinion for a unanimous Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that specific performance of an unlawful plea agreement would be inconsistent with both the sentencing authority of courts and the separation of powers as it would allow courts to imposes sentences outside the range authorized by the legislature. Thus, the Court held that the only remedy available to a defendant who has agreed to a plea agreement that is contrary to law is withdrawal of their plea.

title: Washington v. Ford
facts: Following jury deliberations in respondent Tyrone Ford’s trial on two charges of third degree child rape in the Superior Court for Clark County, the jury initially returned a verdict of guilty on the second charge but left the verdict form for the first charge blank. After being instructed by the judge to enter a verdict, the jury returned to the jury room and subsequently found Ford guilty of the first charge as well. Ford appealed his conviction, asserting that he had been denied a fair trial insofar as the judge had improperly interfered with the verdict when he directed the jury to complete the verdict form for the first charge rather than accept the blank verdict form as an indication of the jury’s inability to reach a verdict with regard to the first charge. The Washington Court of Appeals vacated Ford’s conviction on the first charge, ruling that the judge’s instruction represented a manifest constitutional error that was substantially likely to have affected the outcome of the trial. The state of Washington appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did the trial court improperly interfere with the verdict when it directed the jury to complete the verdict form for the first charge after the jury had initially left the verdict form for the first charge blank?
conclusions: Justice Charles W. Johnson’s opinion for the Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals and reinstated Ford’s conviction, concluding that no improper influence or coercion had occurred insofar as the jury had completed its deliberations and indicated to the judge that it had reached a unanimous verdict prior to the judge’s instruction to complete the verdict form for the first charge. Thus, given the fact that the jury returned less than five minutes later with a completed verdict form, the Court held that there was no indication that its deliberative process had been interfered with or that the blank verdict form had been anything other than an error.

title: Washington v. Hager
facts: Respondent Timothy Hager was convicted of rape in the Superior Court for Pierce County after a trial in which the police officer that had questioned Hager prior to his arrest testified that Hager was evasive during questioning. Hager subsequently appealed his conviction, asserting that a mistrial should have been declared despite the fact that the judge had instructed the jury to disregard the remark as the police officer’s testimony violated his right under the 5th Amendment to the United States Constitution and Article I §9 of the Washington State Constitution against self-incrimination. The Washington Court of Appeals vacated Hager’s conviction, ruling that the trial court had abused its discretion in rejecting Hager’s motion for a mistrial. The state of Washington appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did the police officer’s testimony that Hager was evasive during questioning so prejudice Hager that nothing short of a new trial could ensure fairness?
conclusions: Justice Alexander’s opinion for the Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals and reinstated Hager’s conviction, concluding that Hager’s right against self-incrimination had not been violated by the police officer’s testimony insofar as Hager had not exercised his right to remain silent but rather had responded to questioning. Thus, although the police officer’s expression of an opinion regarding Hager’s credibility was nonetheless prejudicial, the Court held that the judge’s instruction to the jury to disregard the remark was sufficiently curative.

title: Washington v. Thorgerson
facts: Petitioner Kenneth Thorgerson was convicted of child molestation in the Superior Court for Snohomish County. Thorgerson subsequently appealed his conviction, asserting that the prosecutor committed misconduct when he made reference in his opening and closing statements to out of court statements made by the alleged victim that were consistent with her testimony in an effort to bolster her credibility, attempted in his closing statement to shift the burden of proof to the defense, and impugned defense counsel. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Thorgerson’s conviction. Thorgerson appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did the prosecution commit misconduct in its opening and closing statements? If so, was the error harmless?
conclusions: Chief Justice Madsen’s opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that although the prosecutor’s references to out of court statements made by the alleged victim improperly bolstered her credibility and although the prosecutor also improperly attempted to impugn defense counsel, it is unlikely that either instance of misconduct altered the outcome of the proceeding. The Court also held that the prosecutor’s comment upon the failure of the defense to impeach the alleged victim’s testimony did not improperly attempt to shift the burden of proof to the defense.

title: Washington v. Jones
facts: Petitioner Cliff Jones was convicted of first degree child molestation in the Superior Court for Kitsap County and sentenced to 130 months imprisonment and 36 months of community custody. Upon appeal, Jones’s sentence was reduced to 51 months imprisonment and 36 months of community custody after the state of Washington conceded that his offender score had been improperly calculated by the trial court. As Jones had already been imprisoned for 81 months at this point, he was ordered released. Jones subsequently filed a motion for relief from judgment, asserting that the 30 months in excess of his sentence that he had been imprisoned should be credited toward the 36 months of community custody to which he had also been sentenced. The trial court rejected Jones’s motion, ruling that under Washington Revised Code §9.94A.170(3) the term of community custody tolled while Jones was imprisoned. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed the trial court’s ruling. Jones appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does the excess time Jones was imprisoned entitle him to credit reducing his term of community custody?
conclusions: Justice Fairhurst’s opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that imprisonment, even if in excess of an offender’s sentence, cannot satisfy a sentence of community custody given that §9.94A.170(3) tolls sentences of community custody while offenders are confined for any reason and given that Washington Revised Code §9.94A.030(4) requires that community custody be served in the community.

title: Kittitas County v. Eastern Washington Growth Management Hearings Board
facts: Petitioner Kittitas County appealed the respondent Eastern Washington Growth Management Hearings Board’s decision that updates to the county’s comprehensive plan fail to comply with the requirements of the Growth Management Act (Washington Revised Code §36.70A), asserting that the board misinterpreted the law and acted arbitrarily, capriciously, and without substantial evidence in making its findings regarding rural and agricultural densities and uses, zoning techniques, land use near airports, and water resources. The Washington Court of Appeals certified the case to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did the board properly find that updates to Kittitas County’s comprehensive plan fail to comply with the requirements of the Growth Management Act?
conclusions: Justice Owens’ opinion for the Court affirmed in part and reversed in part the board’s decision, concluding that the board did not improperly disregard evidence presented by Kittitas County insofar as the evidence presented was not dispositive of the issues raised, that the board properly found that Kittitas County failed to develop a written record explaining the rural element of its updated comprehensive plan, and that the board properly found that the updated comprehensive plan fails to protect rural character in rural areas, fails to provide for a variety of densities, allows impermissible uses in a designated agricultural area, and fails to protect water resources. However, the Court also held that the board improperly found that the updated comprehensive plan’s airport zone is non-compliant with the Growth Management Act.

title: Veit v. Burlington Northern Santa Fe Corporation
facts: After being injured in an automobile accident with a train operated by respondent Burlington Northern Santa Fe Corporation, petitioner Alizon Veit filed suit against Burlington Northern Santa Fe in the Superior Court for Whatcom County, asserting that Burlington Northern Santa Fe had been negligent in operating the train. The trial court granted summary judgment for Burlington Northern Santa Fe with regard to the issue of excessive speed, ruling that regardless of the fact that the train was traveling in excess of Burlington Northern Santa Fe’s internal speed limit, Veit’s claim of excessive speed was preempted by federal law insofar as the train was traveling below the federal speed limit. The trial court also granted Burlington Northern Santa Fe’s motion in limine to exclude evidence relating to Veit’s compliance with Washington Revised Code §46.61.345, which requires motorists to stop within fifteen to fifty feet of the nearest rail if a stop sign is present. After the jury returned a verdict for Burlington Northern Santa Fe, Veit appealed the trial court’s rulings. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed both the grant of summary judgment with regard to the issue of excessive speed and the grant of the motion in limine precluding Veit from referencing §46.61.345. Veit appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Is Veit’s claim of excessive speed preempted by federal law? Did the trial court err in excluding evidence relating to Veit’s compliance with Washington Revised Code §46.61.345?
conclusions: Chief Justice Madsen’s opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that the Federal Railroad Safety Act (49 U.S.C. §20106), whose speed limit the train that collided with Veit’s automobile was traveling within, occupies the field with regard to train speed and therefore preempts Veit’s excessive speed claim despite the fact that the train was traveling in excess of Burlington Northern Santa Fe’s internal speed limit. The Court also held that any error that the trial court may have committed in excluding evidence relating to Veit’s compliance with Washington Revised Code §46.61.345 was harmless given that the jury found no negligence on the part of Burlington Northern Santa Fe, making the issue of whether there had been contributory negligence on Veit’s part irrelevant.

title: Michaels v. CH2M Hill, Inc.
facts: Respondent Larry Michaels filed suit against petitioner CH2M Hill, Inc. in the Superior Court for Spokane County after being injured in an accident at a sewage treatment plant operated by the city of Spokane that was caused by CH2M Hill recommending, in its capacity as a consultant for a project to upgrade and retrofit the plant, that flows of heated and unheated sludge be separated. The trial court ruled for Michaels. CH2M Hill appealed the trial court’s decision, asserting that it was immune from liability under the Industrial Insurance Act’s conferral of immunity upon design professionals performing professional services on construction projects in Washington Revised Code §51.24.035(1), that it owed no duty to Michaels, and that it was not the proximate cause of Michaels’ injuries given the city’s negligent and reckless operation of the plant. The Washington Court of Appeals certified the case to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Is CH2M Hill immune from liability to Michaels under §51.24.035(1)? If not, did CH2M Hill owe a duty to Michaels that it breached? Was the separation of heated and unheated sludge pursuant to CH2M Hill’s recommendation the proximate cause of Michaels’ injuries?
conclusions: Justice Chambers’ opinion for the Court affirmed the trial court, concluding that although §51.24.035(1) confers immunity upon design professionals performing professional services on construction projects, the mere fact that construction was taking place in other areas of the plant did not render the entire plant a construction site. The Court also held that CH2M did owe a duty to Michaels that it breached insofar as design professionals owe a duty of care to exercise the degree of skill, care, and learning possessed by members of their profession in the community that extends to those working on a property at the time a design is being implemented and that substantial evidence supported the trial court’s conclusion that this duty had been breached. Finally, the Court found that substantial evidence supported the trial court’s conclusion that CH2M Hill’s recommendation that heated and unheated sludge be separated was the proximate cause of Michaels’ injuries and that negligent and reckless operation of the plant on the part of the city was not a superseding cause.

title: Washington v. Martin
facts: Petitioner Timothy Martin was convicted of kidnapping and robbery in the Superior Court for Snohomish County after a trial in which the prosecutor implied during their cross-examination of Martin that Martin had tailored his testimony in response to the testimony of previous witnesses. Martin subsequently appealed his conviction, asserting that the prosecutor’s implication violated his right under Article I §22 of the Washington State Constitution to attend trial and to testify. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Martin’s conviction, holding that the rights conferred by Article I §22 are coextensive with those conferred by the 6th Amendment to the United States Constitution, which the United States Supreme Court held in Portuondo v. Agard does not preclude prosecutors from drawing attention to the fact that the defendant has had an opportunity to hear all of the witnesses testify and tailor their testimony accordingly. Martin appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Are the rights conferred by Article I §22 coextensive with those conferred by the 6th Amendment? If not, were Martin’s rights under Article I §22 violated when the prosecutor implied that Martin had tailored his testimony in response to the testimony of previous witnesses?
conclusions: Justice Alexander’s opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals on alternate grounds, concluding that Article I §22 confers a broader right upon defendants than does the 6th Amendment insofar as the text of Article I §22 explicitly confers several rights not specifically set forth in the 6th Amendment, insofar as historical evidence suggests that the framers of Article I §22 intended to confer a right broader than that conferred by the 6th Amendment, and insofar as some Washington courts have held that Article I §22 precludes the state from drawing attention to the fact that the defendant has had an opportunity to hear all of the witnesses testify in order to imply that the defendant has tailored their testimony. However, despite the fact that Article I §22 confers a broader right upon defendants than does the 6th Amendment, the Court nonetheless held that this right was not violated by the prosecutor’s cross-examination of Martin as the prosecutor’s questions had been elicited by Martin’s reference to previous testimony and as prohibiting such questions would inhibit the jury’s ability to judge credibility.

title: Seattle v. May
facts: Petitioner Robert May was convicted in the Seattle Municipal Court of violating a no contact order that prohibited him from contacting his former wife. May appealed his conviction, asserting that the no contact order was invalid insofar as the superior court that issued it failed to make the required finding that he was likely to resume acts of domestic violence that was necessary for the duration of the order to extend beyond one year and that the no contact order failed to provide notice that violating it would be a criminal offense. The Superior Court for King County reversed May’s conviction, holding that the no contact order was facially defective. However, this decision was subsequently reversed by the Washington Court of Appeals, which reinstated May’s conviction. May appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Was the no contact order issued against May valid? Did the no contact order provide adequate notice that violating it would be a criminal offense?
conclusions: Justice Owens’ opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that the collateral bar rule precludes a collateral challenge to the validity of a no contact order in a proceeding for violation of the no contact order unless the no contact order is void for lack of jurisdiction. Thus, as the superior court that issued the no contact order had jurisdiction to issue such orders, the Court held that May cannot challenge the validity of the no contact order regardless of its erroneousness. The Court also found that the no contact order did provide adequate notice that violating it would be a criminal offense by referencing Washington Revised Code §26.50.110, which criminalizes all violations of no contact and protection orders.

title: Blair v. TravelCenters of America
facts: Petitioner Maureen Blair filed suit against respondent TravelCenters of America in the Superior Court for King County after injuring herself by slipping and falling on a gasoline spill in the parking lot of a truck stop operated by TravelCenters of America. After Blair failed to timely submit a complete list of witnesses she planned to call at trial, the trial court struck two of the witnesses that had been untimely added and granted TravelCenters of America’s motion for summary judgment on grounds that Blair could not prove causation in the absence of the two witnesses that had been struck. Blair subsequently appealed the trial court’s granting of summary judgment for TravelCenters of America, asserting that the trial court had abused its discretion in striking the two witnesses without setting forth the reasons for its ruling. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed the trial court’s decision. Blair appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Was the trial court required to set forth its reasons for striking Blair’s untimely submitted witnesses?
conclusions: Justice Stephens’ opinion for the Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that the trial court was required to consider the willfulness of the violation of the rules of discovery, the degree of prejudice arising from the violation, and the sufficiency of lesser sanctions and to make a formal record demonstrating its consideration of these factors prior to striking untimely submitted witnesses. Thus, as the trial court had made no findings on the record prior to striking Blair’s witnesses, the Court vacated the trial court’s order and its subsequent granting of summary judgment and remanded the case.

title: Washington v. Wilson
facts: After reaching a plea agreement with prosecutors, petitioner Jason Wilson pled guilty to two counts of identity theft in the Superior Court for Grays Harbor County and was sentenced. When it was subsequently revealed that Wilson's offender score had been improperly calculated insofar as a previous conviction for a gross misdemeanor had been counted as a felony conviction and that Wilson's sentence was therefore erroneous, Wilson moved to be resentenced. The trial court denied Wilson's motion, ruling that Wilson's only remedy was to withdraw his guilty plea. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals concluded that Wilson's offender score had in fact been correctly calculated and affirmed Wilson's sentence on grounds that Washington Revised Code §9.94A.525(4) requires anticipatory offenses to be scored the same as if they were convictions for completed offenses in calculating offender scores. Wilson appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does §9.94A.525(4) require anticipatory offenses to be scored the same as if they were convictions for completed offenses in calculating offender scores? If not, is Wilson entitled to be resentenced?
conclusions: Justice Charles W. Johnson's opinion for a unanimous Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals, holding that §9.94A.525(4) only requires an anticipatory offense to be scored the same as if it were a conviction for a completed offense in calculating an offender score when the anticipatory offense is itself a felony. As Wilson's offender score had therefore been improperly calculated, the Court also concluded that the trial court's error had been an error of law rather than an error of fact and that Wilson was therefore entitled to be resentenced despite his consent to the plea agreement.

title: Washington v. Robinson
facts: Petitioner Michael Robinson was convicted of burglary, theft of a firearm, unlawful possession of a firearm, and possession of methamphetamine after a search of an automobile he was riding in following its driver’s apprehension for reckless driving revealed stolen property. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals dismissed the conviction for possession of methamphetamine but affirmed Robinson’s other convictions. In the interim, the United States Supreme Court ruled in Arizona v. Gant that warrantless searches of automobiles incident to arrest are permissible only in instances in which the arrestee is unsecured and within reaching distance of the automobile’s passenger compartment or in which there is reason to believe that evidence relevant to the crime of arrest may be found in the automobile. Asserting that neither of these exceptions applied to the search that led to his arrest, Robinson subsequently appealed his conviction to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: May a defendant challenge a search for the first time on appeal following a change in constitutional interpretation?
conclusions: Justice Owens’ opinion for the Court vacated Robinson’s conviction and remanded the case to the trial court for a suppression hearing, concluding that although Robinson had not challenged the constitutionality of the search either at trial or upon his initial appeal, the principles of issue preservation that would ordinarily bar him from raising the issue for the first time on appeal do not apply in cases in which a new controlling interpretation material to the defendant’s case that overrules existing precedent is issued subsequent to the defendant’s trial.

title: In re personal restraint of Nichols
facts: Petitioner Glenn Nichols was convicted of possession of cocaine with intent to deliver and possession of marijuana in the Superior Court for King County after a hotel desk clerk identified Nichols to police officers as the occupant of a hotel room in which a cocaine purchase had occurred, the officers discovered that Nichols’ driver’s license was suspended, and the officers proceeded to arrest Nichols for driving with a suspended driver’s license and discovered cocaine and marijuana in a search of Nichols’ person incident to the arrest. Nichols appealed his convictions on grounds unrelated to the constitutionality of the warrantless search of the hotel registry that led to his arrest. While this direct appeal was stayed pending the Supreme Court of Washington’s decision in Surge v. Washington, Nichols filed a personal restraint petition in the Washington Court of Appeals asserting that the warrantless search of the hotel registry violated his rights under the 4th Amendment to the United States Constitution and Article I §7 of the Washington State Constitution. In the interim, the Supreme Court of Washington decided in Washington v. Jorden that random warrantless searches of hotel registries intended to ascertain if there are outstanding arrest warrants for any of the guests are inconsistent with Article I §7. Following the Supreme Court of Washington’s decision in Surge v. Washington, the Washington Court of Appeals lifted the stay and subsequently affirmed Nichols’ convictions. It also lifted the stay on Nichols’ personal restraint petition and dismissed it. Nichols appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: May Nichols raise an objection to the warrantless search of the hotel registry for the first time in a personal restraint petition? If so, did the warrantless search of the hotel registry violate Nichols’ rights under Article I §7?
conclusions: Justice Alexander’s opinion for the Court concluded that although Nichols had not raised the issue of the constitutionality of the search either at trial or upon direct appeal, he could nonetheless raise the issue for the first time in a personal restraint petition as a constitutional issue may be raised for the time in a personal restraint petition if actual prejudice is demonstrated. However, the Court also held that the warrantless search of the hotel registry did not violate Nichols’ rights under Article I §7 given that, unlike the warrantless search of a hotel registry that was ruled unconstitutional by the Court in Washington v. Jorden, the search was not random and was based upon individualized suspicion that drug trafficking was occurring in the hotel room. Thus, the Court affirmed Nichols’ convictions.

title: Mills v. Western Washington University
facts: Respondent Perry Mills, a professor at Western Washington University, was suspended without pay for two academic quarters following a hearing before a university disciplinary panel that concluded that Mills had engaged in a pattern of abusive and inappropriate behavior toward students and faculty. Mills subsequently filed suit against Western Washington University in the Superior Court for Whatcom County, asserting that Western Washington University had violated Washington’s Administrative Procedure Act (Washington Revised Code §34.05) and Article I §10 of the Washington State Constitution by closing the hearing to the public. The trial court denied relief. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals reversed the trial court’s decision and ordered a new hearing, ruling that the Adminstrative Procedure Act required that Mills’ hearing be open to the public. Western Washington University appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does the Administrative Procedure Act allow faculty disciplinary hearings to be closed to the public? If so, does Article I §10 nonetheless require that such hearings be open to the public?
conclusions: Justice Alexander’s opinion for a unanimous Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that although the Administrative Procedure Act generally requires that all hearings be open to public observation, Western Washington University was authorized to conduct a private hearing by Washington Revised Code §28B.10.648(2), which permits institutions of higher education to promulgate their own rules and regulations for peer review proceedings. The Court also held that Article I §10, which requires that justice in all cases be administered openly, does not apply to quasi-judicial disciplinary hearings conducted by state agencies such as universities.

title: Beggs v. Fregeau
facts: Following Tyler DeLeon’s death as a result of neglect and abuse by his adoptive mother, petitioner Breean Beggs and his other adoptive siblings filed suit against respondent David Fregeau in the Superior Court for Spokane County, alleging that Fregeau, as DeLeon’s physician, had been aware of the neglect and abuse and that he was therefore liable for medical malpractice and failure to report suspected child abuse. The trial court granted summary judgment for Fregeau, ruling that Beggs and the other adoptive siblings are not dependents entitled to bring wrongful death and survival claims on DeLeon’s behalf and that Washington Revised Code §26.44.030, which mandates the reporting of suspected child abuse, does not imply a cause of action against healthcare providers. Beggs appealed this decision to the Washington Court of Appeals, which certified the case to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does §26.44.030 imply a cause of action against healthcare providers who fail to report suspected child abuse? If so, are Beggs and DeLeon’s other adoptive siblings dependents of DeLeon entitled to bring wrongful death and survival claims on DeLeon’s behalf?
conclusions: Justice Sanders’ opinion for the Court affirmed in part and reversed in part the trial court’s decision, concluding that while §26.44.030 does imply a cause of action against healthcare providers who fail to report suspected child abuse given that victims of child abuse are within the class for whose benefit the statute was enacted, that the statute implicitly creates a civil remedy, and that an implied cause of action is consistent with the purposes of the statute, Beggs and the other adoptive siblings were not financially dependent upon DeLeon and therefore are not entitled to bring wrongful death and survival claims on his behalf as they were not substantially dependent upon the support payments DeLeon received from the state of Washington. Thus, the Court affirmed the granting of summary judgment.

title: Hardee v. Department of Social and Health Services
facts: Petitioner Kathleen Hardee’s home child care license was revoked by the respondent Department of Social and Health Services after Hardee’s son sexually assaulted a child in Hardee’s home and a subsequent investigation by the Department of Social and Health Services revealed that Hardee’s son had had unsupervised access to children under Hardee’s care in violation of a safety plan imposed in response to his previous convictions for harassment, intimidation, and assault. After administrative review affirmed the revocation, Hardee appealed the Department of Social and Health Services’ decision first to the Superior Court for King County and then to the Washington Court of Appeals, both of which also affirmed the revocation. Hardee appealed to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does due process require that decisions by the Department of Social and Health Services to revoke home child care licenses be supported by clear and convincing evidence rather than by a preponderance of the evidence?
conclusions: Justice James M. Johnson’s opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that Washington Revised Code §43.215.300(2), which requires that decisions to revoke home child care licenses be supported by a preponderance of the evidence, does not deny those deprived of home child care licenses due process given the relatively minimal time, expense, and education required to obtain such a license and the continued ability of those deprived of home child care licenses to work in the field as child care staff members, the low risk of erroneous deprivation and the relatively low value of additional procedural safeguards, and the state’s compelling interest in protecting the safety of children receiving in home child care without being held to a burden of proof that may result in the endangerment of children.

title: Dolan v. King County
facts: Respondent Kevin Dolan, a public defender employed by a non-profit organization contracted by petitioner King County to provide legal services for indigent defendants, filed suit against King County in the Superior Court for Pierce County on behalf of himself and others similarly situated in an effort to obtain the right to enroll in the state’s Public Employees Retirement System. The trial court certified the question of whether the public defenders are de facto state employees eligible to enroll in the Public Employees Retirement System to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Are employees of public defender organizations contracted by King County to provide legal services for indigent defendants de facto state employees eligible to enroll in the Public Employees Retirement System?
conclusions: Justice Chambers’ opinion for the Court concluded that Dolan and the other public defenders are de facto state employees eligible to enroll in the Public Employees Retirement System given the control exercised by King County over the public defender organizations. In particular, as King County provides virtually all of the public defender organizations’ funding, establishes pay scales for their employees, and bars them from accepting other clients or leasing or acquiring property without the county’s consent, the Court found that the public defender organizations function as de facto county agencies.

title: Samantha A. v. Department of Social and Health Services
facts: Respondent Samantha A., a child who suffers from a host of medical problems and receives in home Medicaid personal care, filed suit against the petitioner Department of Social and Health Services in the Superior Court for Thurston County, asserting that Washington Administrative Code §388-106-0213, which provides for automatic reductions in the number of hours of Medicaid personal care received by children based upon their age and whether or not they live with their parents, violates 42 U.S.C. §1396a(a)(10)(B)(i)’s Medicaid comparability requirements. The trial court ruled for Samantha A. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals transferred the case to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does §388-106-0213 violate Medicaid comparability requirements?
conclusions: Justice Charles W. Johnson’s opinion for the Court affirmed the trial court, concluding that §388-106-0213 violates Medicaid comparability requirements by reducing benefits on the basis of considerations other than recipients’ actual need and by failing to consider whether a child’s needs will continue to be met after the reduction.

title: Tacoma News, Inc. v. Cayce
facts: Judge James Cayce of the Superior Court for King County presided over the taking of a deposition from a witness in a criminal trial in an empty courtroom. In response to a motion by defense counsel, Cayce agreed to close the courtroom to non-parties. Tacoma News, Inc., whose representatives had attempted to enter the courtroom during the deposition but were refused entry, subsequently petitioned the Supreme Court of Washington for a writ of mandamus compelling Cayce to open the deposition to the public, asserting that closing the taking of the deposition had violated both Article I §10 of the Washington State Constitution’s guarantee of the open administration of justice and the 1st Amendment to the United States Constitution’s implicit guarantee of public access to criminal trials.
questions: Was the deposition subject to Article I §10’s guarantee of the open administration of justice? Did closing the courtroom during the taking of the deposition violate the 1st Amendment’s implicit guarantee of public access to criminal trials?
conclusions: Chief Justice Madsen’s opinion for the Court rejected Tacoma News’s petition for a writ of mandamus, concluding that discovery is not subject to Article I §10 and that the mere fact that the deposition was taken in a courtroom with a judge present due to the fact that the witness was being held in the county jail at the time did not render the deposition a judicial proceeding open to the public. The Court also held that closing the courtroom during the taking of the deposition did not violate the 1st Amendment’s implicit guarantee of public access to criminal trials insofar as this guarantee does not extend to discovery.

title: Washington v. Sims
facts: Petitioner Jack Sims pled guilty to child molestation in the Superior Court for Cowlitz County and, pursuant to a special sex offender sentencing alternative, was sentenced to a suspended sixty month sentence contingent upon compliance with crime-related prohibitions that included an order that Sims neither reside in nor enter Cowlitz County. Sims subsequently appealed the order on grounds that it was not narrowly tailored and therefore unconstitutional. The Washington Court of Appeals agreed, vacated Sims’ sentence in its entirety, and remanded the case to the trial court for resentencing. Sims appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington, asserting that the scope of the remand should have been limited to revision of the unconstitutional crime-related prohibition.
questions: Did the Washington Court of Appeals err in failing to limit the scope of the remand to revision of the unconstitutional crime-related prohibition?
conclusions: Justice Owens’ opinion for the Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that Sims’ sentence was not properly before the Washington Court of Appeals insofar as Sims’ appeal had been limited to the order barring him from residing in or entering Cowlitz County, which was separable from his sentence, and insofar as the state had not filed a cross appeal. Thus, as to hold otherwise would have a potentially chilling effect upon defendants exercising their right to appeal, the Court remanded the case to the trial court for revision of the unconstitutional crime-related prohibition.

title: Snohomish County Public Transportation Benefit Area Corporation v. FirstGroup America, Inc.
facts: The petitioner Snohomish County Public Transportation Benefit Area Corporation, doing business as Community Transit, entered into a contract with respondent FirstGroup America, Inc., doing business as First Transit, under which First Transit agreed to provide bus services between Snohomish County and parts of King County for Community Transit. The contract included an indemnity provision requiring that First Transit indemnify Community Transit for any losses occasioned in whole or in part by the presence of First Transit buses except for those resulting solely from the negligence of Community Transit. Following a multiple vehicle accident involving a Community Transit bus, a First Transit bus, and two other automobiles that was caused by the shared negligence of the driver of the Community Transit bus and the driver of one of the other automobiles, Community Transit tendered a claim of indemnification to First Transit. After First Transit refused to indemnify Community Transit, Community Transit settled the claims against it by the drivers of the other automobiles and filed suit against First Transit in the Superior Court for Snohomish County, asserting that First Transit had breached the contract. The trial court granted summary judgment for First Transit. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals affirmed. Community Transit appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does the contract clearly and unequivocally require First Transit to indemnify against losses caused by Community Transit’s negligence?
conclusions: Chief Justice Madsen’s opinion for the Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that the contract’s indemnification provision is enforceable insofar as it clearly and unequivocally shows intent to indemnify Community Transit against claims and losses that result from its own negligence so long as it is not solely negligent.

title: Bainbridge Island Police Guild v. Koenig
facts: Petitioner Kim Koenig filed a public records request pursuant to the Public Records Act (Washington Revised Code §42.56) for records relating to the Puyallup Police Department’s investigation of her allegation that an officer of the Bainbridge Island Police Department sexually assaulted her, an investigation that resulted in no charges being filed. The respondent Bainbridge Island Police Guild subsequently petitioned the Superior Court for Pierce County to enjoin the Puyallup Police Department from producing the records, asserting that they were exempt from production under §42.56.230(2)’s personal information exemption insofar as the request was specific to records relating to the investigation of Koenig’s allegation against the officer and that production, even if the officer’s name were redacted, would indirectly reveal his identity in relation to the incident in violation of his right to privacy. The trial court granted the injunction, ruling that the records were exempt in their entirety. Koenig appealed this decision directly to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Are the records exempt in their entirety under §42.56230(2)’s personal information exemption? If not, are the records exempt in their entirety under the Criminal Records Privacy Act (Washington Revised Code §10.97)?
conclusions: Justice Fairhurst’s opinion for the Court reversed the trial court, concluding that although the production of the officer’s identity in connection with an unsubstantiated allegation of sexual assault would violate their right to privacy insofar as it would be highly offensive and insofar as the public does not have a legitimate interest in the officer’s identity due to the unsubstantiated nature of the allegations, the public does have a legitimate interest in the conduct of the police investigation of such allegations. Thus, the Court ordered that the records be released, albeit with the officer’s name redacted. The Court also held that doing so would not violate §10.97 given that §10.97 requires nothing more than the redaction of the officer’s identity as the remaining summary of the police investigation is not criminal history record information.

title: In re personal restraint of Scott
facts: Respondent Joshua Scott was convicted of first degree robbery, unlawful possession of a firearm, and possession of stolen property. On the basis of the jury’s finding by special verdict that Scott was armed with a deadly weapon during the commission of these crimes, a firearm enhancement was added to Scott’s sentence. Following the Supreme Court of Washington’s subsequent decision in Washington v. Recuenco that the erroneous imposition of a firearm enhancement on the basis of a deadly weapon special verdict is not subject to harmless error analysis, Scott filed an untimely personal restraint petition that asserted that his sentence is invalid on its face. The Washington Court of Appeals vacated Scott’s sentence, holding that Scott’s sentence is invalid on its face under Recuenco because it did not mirror the special verdict form and because of the lack of a written finding that Scott was armed. The state of Washington appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does the rule announced in Recuenco apply retroactively to Scott’s sentence?
conclusions: Justice Chambers’ opinion for the Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that the rule announced in Recuenco does not apply retroactively to Scott’s sentence insofar as the question of whether the judge or the jury determines whether a defendant is armed with a firearm rather than merely a deadly weapon does not implicate the observance of procedures implicit in the concept of ordered liberty.

title: Washington v. Coucil
facts: Petitioner Nikeemia Coucil was charged with felony harassment in the Superior Court for King County and released on bail pending trial. After Coucil subsequently failed to appear for a pretrial hearing, he was also charged with bail jumping. Following his apprehension, Coucil was ultimately convicted of the lesser crime of misdemeanor harassment and, in a separate trial, of bail jumping. At sentencing, the trial court classified the bail jumping conviction as a felony on grounds that Coucil was being charged with a felony at the time he failed to appear. Coucil appealed his sentence, asserting that the bail jumping conviction should have been classified as a misdemeanor given that, despite initially being charged with felony, he was ultimately convicted of a misdemeanor. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Coucil's sentence, holding that Washington Revised Code §9A.76.170 classifies bail jumping for sentencing purposes according to nature of the underlying charge at the time the defendant fails to appear rather than according to the nature of the underlying charge's ultimate disposition. Coucil appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Is the penalty imposed for bail jumping pursuant to §9A.76.170 contingent upon the nature of the underlying charge at the time the defendant fails to appear or upon the nature of the underlying charge's ultimate disposition?
conclusions: Justice Alexander's opinion for a unanimous Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that §9A.76.170 unambiguously bases the penalty for bail jumping upon the nature of the underlying charge at the time the defendant fails to appear as to hold otherwise would prevent bail jumping charges from being litigated until underlying charges were litigated.

title: Z.D.I. Gaming, Inc. v. Washington State Gambling Commission
facts: Respondent Z.D.I. Gaming, Inc. filed an application with the petitioner Washington State Gambling Commission requesting permission to distribute a new type of electronic gaming machine that it had developed. After the Washington State Gambling Commission denied the application on grounds that the machine’s use of a “cash card” violates Washington Administrative Code §230-30-070’s requirement that all prizes be awarded in either cash or merchandise, Z.D.I. Gaming petitioned the Superior Court for Pierce County for judicial review. The Washington State Gambling Commission moved for dismissal, asserting that Washington Revised Code §9.46.095 confers exclusive subject matter jurisdiction over cases in which the Washington State Gambling Commission is a party upon the Superior Court for Thurston County. The superior court denied the motion to dismiss but transferred the case to the Superior Court for Thurston County, which reversed the Washington State Gambling Commission’s denial of Z.D.I. Gaming’s application. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals affirmed, holding that dismissal was not required insofar as §9.46.095 relates to venue rather than subject matter jurisdiction and that the Washington State Gambling Commission’s denial of Z.D.I. Gaming’s application was not supported by substantial evidence. The Washington State Gambling Commission appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does §9.46.095 confer exclusive subject matter jurisdiction over cases in which the Washington State Gambling Commission is a party upon the Superior Court for Thurston County? If not, was the Washington State Gambling Commission’s denial of Z.D.I. Gaming’s application supported by substantial evidence?
conclusions: Justice Chambers’ opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that Article IV §6 of Washington State Constitution precludes the legislature from withdrawing original jurisdiction from superior courts and that §9.46.095 must therefore be interpreted as relating to venue rather than subject matter jurisdiction. The Court also held that the Washington State Gambling Commission erred in denying Z.D.I. Gaming’s application.

title: Seattle v. McKenna
facts: Following the enaction of the federal Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act, Attorney General Robert McKenna and the attorneys general of twelve other states jointly filed a lawsuit in federal court challenging the constitutionality of the law. The city of Seattle subsequently petitioned the Supreme Court of Washington for a writ of mandamus compelling McKenna to withdraw the state of Washington from the litigation.
questions: Does the attorney general possess common law or implied power under the Washington State Constitution to initiate litigation on behalf of the state? If not, is McKenna’s participation in the litigation authorized by statute?
conclusions: Justice Owens’ opinion for the Court denied the petition for a writ of mandamus, concluding that although the attorney general possesses neither common law power nor implied power under Article III §21 of the Washington State Constitution to initiate litigation on behalf of the state, Washington Revised Code §43.10.030’s grant of authority for the attorney general to appear for and represent the state in all cases in which the state is interested authorizes McKenna’s participation in the litigation.

title: Goldmark v. McKenna
facts: Seeking to condemn an easement for the installation and maintenance of a power line over public lands, Public Utility District #1 of Okanogan County filed an action against Commissioner of Public Lands Peter Goldmark in the Superior Court for Okanogan County. The superior court granted summary judgment for Public Utility District #1. Although Goldmark wished to appeal the superior court’s decision, Attorney General Robert McKenna, based upon his evaluation of the merits of the case, refused to pursue the case. Goldmark subsequently petitioned the Supreme Court of Washington for a writ of mandamus compelling McKenna to appeal the superior court’s decision.
questions: Does the attorney general have a statutory duty to provide the commissioner of public lands with legal representation?
conclusions: Justice Charles W. Johnson’s opinion for the Court granted the writ of mandamus, concluding that the attorney general is required by Washington Revised Code §43.12.075 to institute or defend any action or proceeding when requested to do so by the commissioner of public lands and that this duty is not limited to representing the commissioner of public lands at the trial court level and also extends to the appellate level.

title: Optimer International, Inc. v. R.P. Bellevue, L.L.C.
facts: Pursuant to a clause in its lease with respondent R.P. Bellevue, L.L.C., petitioner Optimer International, Inc. submitted a demand for arbitration after a dispute arose regarding whether R.P. Bellevue had violated certain lease provisions. After an arbitrator subsequently concluded that R.P. Bellevue had violated the lease and awarded Optimer International damages, R.P. Bellevue sought review of the arbitrator's decision in the Superior Court for King County. The superior court rejected R.P. Bellevue's motion, ruling that a clause in the lease declaring the arbitrator's decision final and non-appealable and enforceable represented a waiver of any right to judicial review. R.P. Bellevue appealed the superior court's decision, asserting that the right to judicial review of arbitration awards conferred by the Washington Arbitration Act (Washington Revised Code §7.04) cannot be waived. The Washington Court of Appeals reversed the superior court, holding that the clause in the lease foreclosing judicial review is unenforceable. Optimer International appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: May the right to judicial review of an arbitration award be waived?
conclusions: Justice Owens' opinion for a unanimous Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that as arbitration exists as an alternative form of dispute resolution solely by virtue of statutory provisions in §7.04 authorizing it, §7.04's provisions permitting judicial review of arbitration awards cannot be modified by parties to a contract. Thus, the Court remanded the case to the superior court for review of the arbitrator's decision.
